chapters.title: Limits and continuity
chapters.what: lim f(x) = L means f(x) can be kept as close to L as you like (within ε) by keeping x close enough to a (within δ), without ever needing x = a.
chapters.looks: An ε-band around L and a δ-window around a: the graph inside the window must stay inside the band. In 2D the limit can depend on the path taken to the point.
chapters.change: ▶ shrinks ε a hundredfold: δ shrinks with it but never becomes zero — that is what 'the limit exists' means.
chapters.use: Small-angle approximations, derivatives (limits of slopes), continuous compounding, removing 0/0 in formulas.
misc: The value f(a) is irrelevant to the limit (it may not even exist).
Two paths agreeing does not prove a 2D limit exists.

examples.title: sin x / x → 1: the small-angle approximation
examples.world: sin θ ≈ θ makes a pendulum simple-harmonic and a lens 'paraxial'.

examples.title: (1 + x)^(1/x) → e: continuous compounding
examples.world: Interest compounded ever more often tends to growth by e^r.

examples.title: A slope is a limit: (sin(1 + h) − sin 1)/h → cos 1
examples.world: A speedometer shows the limit of average speeds over shorter and shorter times.

examples.title: A removable gap: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) → 4
examples.world: 0/0 at one point in a formula is often just a hole to fill (L'Hôpital, sinc filters).

examples.title: (e^x − 1)/x → 1: small growth rates
examples.world: For small rates r, e^r − 1 ≈ r: 1% continuous growth is about 1% per year.

examples.title: A 2D limit that depends on the path: xy/(x² + y²)
examples.world: Along y = x it tends to ½, along y = 0 to 0 — so the limit at the origin does not exist.

chapters.title: Differential calculus
chapters.what: The derivative f′(x) is the slope of the tangent: the limit of rise over run. It is a rate (velocity, current, marginal cost) and it vanishes at a smooth maximum or minimum.
chapters.looks: The dashed tangent touches the curve at the probe; its slope is the readout f′. Moving the probe along (▶) shows where f′ changes sign.
chapters.change: Put the probe where f′ = 0 and read f″: its sign tells a hill from a valley.
chapters.use: Velocities and accelerations, optimal design, least-time paths (Snell's law), cooling rates, beam curvature.
misc: f′ = 0 does not guarantee an extremum (x³ at 0).
The derivative of a position in metres per second² is an acceleration, not a speed.

examples.title: The tangent to sin x at x = 1 has slope cos 1
examples.world: Linearising a nonlinear response around an operating point (every control system does this).

examples.title: A dropped ball: velocity is the slope of height
examples.world: h(t) = h₀ − ½ g t²: after 1 s it falls at 9.81 m/s.

examples.title: The biggest open box from a 20 × 20 sheet
examples.world: Cut squares of side x from the corners: V = x(20 − 2x)², largest at x = 10/3.

examples.title: Fermat's least time gives Snell's law
examples.world: Light from air (speed 1) to water (speed 0.75) takes the path of least time; there sin θ₁/sin θ₂ = 4/3.
examples.note: f(x) is the travel time via the crossing point x; its minimum is where the refraction angles obey Snell's law.

examples.title: Newton's law of cooling: the rate is the slope
examples.world: Newton (1701) measured cooling rates proportional to the excess temperature: T = 20 + 60 e^{−kt}.

examples.title: A cantilever's curvature is y″ = M/EI
examples.world: Tip-loaded cantilever: y = −(P/EI) x²(3L − x)/6, so y″(0) = −PL/EI at the wall, where the moment is largest.

chapters.title: Integral calculus
chapters.what: The definite integral adds up f(x) dx: the limit of Riemann sums. The fundamental theorem says it equals F(b) − F(a) for any antiderivative F.
chapters.looks: Rectangles under the curve (2D) become disks of a solid (3D); ▶ refines n and both sums close in on the exact value.
chapters.change: Switch left/right/midpoint/trapezoid/Simpson: at the same n the error drops by orders of magnitude.
chapters.use: Work, energy, impulse, probability, volumes, total quantities from rates.
misc: Area below the axis counts negative.
Simpson's rule is exact for cubics, not just parabolas.

examples.title: Riemann sums for ∫₀² x² dx = 8/3
examples.world: Every numerical integrator starts here.

examples.title: Work to stretch a spring: ∫ kx dx = ½ k x²
examples.world: A 200 N/m spring stretched 10 cm stores 1 J.

examples.title: Simpson's rule is exact for a cubic
examples.world: Engineering codes use Simpson for ship hull areas and volumes.

examples.title: Volume of a paraboloid by disks
examples.world: Revolving y = √x on [0, 4] gives a satellite-dish-shaped bowl of volume 8π.

examples.title: Probability is area: 68% within one standard deviation
examples.world: ∫ of the normal density from −1 to 1 = 0.6827 — the '68-95-99.7 rule'.

examples.title: Impulse of a racket strike: J = ∫ F dt
examples.world: A 5 ms half-sine contact force peaking at 1 kN delivers 3.18 N·s of momentum.

chapters.title: Applications: volumes, parametric curves, polar curves
chapters.what: Integrals measure more than area: volumes of revolution, lengths of curves given as (x(t), y(t)), and areas and lengths of polar curves.
chapters.looks: The point runs along the curve with its velocity and acceleration arrows; the readout accumulates the arc length as it goes.
chapters.change: Change the parameters of the curve and watch the length and the curvature radius respond.
chapters.use: Cable lengths, arches, gear and cam profiles, trajectories, barrels and tanks.
misc: Arc length is not the area under the curve.
A parametric curve can pass the same point twice at different parameter values.

examples.title: The catenary: a hanging chain and the Gateway Arch
examples.world: y = a cosh(x/a); the St Louis arch is an inverted (weighted) catenary.

examples.title: The cycloid: one arch is 8r long
examples.world: A point on a rolling wheel; the brachistochrone, the curve of fastest descent.

examples.title: The cardioid: a microphone's pickup pattern
examples.world: r = 1 + cos θ is the directional pattern of cardioid microphones and some antennas.

examples.title: A projectile's path length
examples.world: Launched at 20 m/s and 45°, it flies 2.88 s and travels 46.8 m along its arc.

examples.title: The volume of a wine barrel by disks
examples.world: Kepler worked out barrel volumes this way; R(x) = 0.30 − 0.395 x² over a 0.9 m length.

chapters.title: Sequences and series
chapters.what: An infinite series is the limit of its partial sums. Taylor series rebuild a smooth function from its derivatives at one point; Fourier series rebuild a periodic function from sines and cosines.
chapters.looks: Partial sums hug the function over a wider and wider range (2D); stacked by N they form a surface that settles onto the true graph (3D).
chapters.change: ▶ adds terms one at a time; watch Taylor fail outside its radius of convergence and Fourier overshoot at a jump (Gibbs).
chapters.use: How calculators compute sin and e^x, signal synthesis, error estimates, approximations in physics.
misc: More terms do not help outside the radius of convergence.
The Gibbs overshoot (~9% of the jump) never goes away; it only narrows.

examples.title: sin x from its Taylor polynomial
examples.world: Maths libraries evaluate sin by range reduction plus a short polynomial.

examples.title: The Gibbs overshoot at a square wave's jump
examples.world: Ringing next to sharp edges in audio and images; Gibbs explained it in 1899.

examples.title: e from 1 + 1 + 1/2! + … + 1/10!
examples.world: Ten terms give e to 8 digits.

examples.title: ln(1 + x) converges only for −1 < x ≤ 1
examples.world: At x = 0.5 twenty terms are plenty; move the probe past 1 and the sums explode.

examples.title: The geometric series and Zeno's paradox
examples.world: ½ + ¼ + … = 1: infinitely many steps, finite distance; also annuities and loan formulas.

examples.title: A bowed string's sawtooth from its harmonics
examples.world: A violin string under the bow moves in a sawtooth (Helmholtz motion); its harmonics fall as 1/k.
